findings.title: addi erroneously writes data memory
findings.behavior: Each addi sets MEMWRITE=1 while MEMREAD=0. DataMemory consequently overwrites memory[rs+signed_immediate] with the pre-write value of rt. Arithmetic results may look correct while unrelated data are corrupted.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 addi arithmetic semantics

findings.title: jump opcode and PC selection path absent
findings.behavior: Opcode 000010 falls into inert default control. The next PC is only PC+4 or a branch target; j cannot redirect execution. Presence of an unused 26-to-28-bit shift module does not implement jump.
findings.requirement: Slides 2-3 include jump for MIPS architecture

findings.title: forwarding does not reach store data
findings.behavior: FORWARDB selects Mux32_1_IN0, but EX_MEM.READ_DATA_2 captures READ_DATA_2_ID_EX rather than that forwarded value. An adjacent producing instruction followed by sw of its destination stores a stale register value. Example: addi r1,r0,5; sw r1,0(r0) stores 0 after reset, although r1 becomes 5.
findings.requirement: Level C hazard handling; exact slide-8 Program 2 only tests forwarded store base and therefore would not expose store-data case

findings.title: taken branches keep younger instructions alive
findings.behavior: beq is resolved from EX/MEM, but IF/ID, ID/EX and EX/MEM are not flushed on a taken branch. Up to three younger instructions from the fall-through path still perform register or memory writes. This requires deliberate NOP scheduling to avoid visible wrong-path effects.
findings.requirement: Slides 2-3 beq semantics; control-hazard policy is not explicitly spelled out in PPT diagrams

findings.title: instruction memory leaves three entries uninitialized
findings.behavior: Reset clears [12..63] but only loads [0..8]. Entries 9,10,11 remain X and are fetched directly after the demo program.
findings.requirement: Slides 3 and 9 executable instruction-memory program and simulation evidence

findings.title: data-memory last entry is not reset
findings.behavior: memory is declared [0:63], but reset loop uses i < 63. memory[63] remains unknown until explicitly written.
findings.requirement: Reset correctness; not an explicit separate PPT requirement

findings.title: supplied instruction programs omit required instruction or hazard coverage
findings.behavior: Pipeline demo contains all listed arithmetic/memory operations and beq, but no jump, and its branch compares unequal values so never validates a taken path. Hazard demo has addi, sub, and, or, add, sw only: no lw, slt, beq, or jump and no load-use hazard stimulus. Its dependency pattern resembles slide 8 but register numbers and sequence differ from the exact pictured program.
findings.requirement: Slides 3,8,9 programs, hazard stimulus, simulation results

findings.title: top testbenches have no correctness assertions
findings.behavior: All benches only generate clock/reset; none checks expected PC, registers, memory, forwarding or stalls. Hazard TB also has no finish and runs indefinitely without external simulation bound.
findings.requirement: Slide 9 top-module testbench is structurally present; these benches alone do not prove functional compliance

findings.title: data memory uses raw word indices and only covers 0..63
findings.behavior: DataMemory directly indexes memory[ADDR], unlike instruction memory which divides PC by 4. Addresses 64 and higher are out of range; the slide-8 example sw r15,100(r2) is out of range with r2=0. This is a documented MIPS byte-address compatibility/capacity limitation, not enough evidence alone to call all in-range lw/sw incorrect.
findings.requirement: MIPS-like memory semantics and slide-8 example; PPT does not mandate a specific memory size/address unit

findings.requirements_caveat: PPTX has deadline 2019/1/15 while source folders contain historical 2020/2024 Vivado artifacts; audit applies this supplied PPTX only and cannot prove requirements are unchanged every year.
findings.summary: All three variants are incomplete or functionally defective against the supplied requirements. Single-cycle is closest in ISA coverage. Pipeline and hazard have the expected pipeline-register structure; hazard additionally has forwarding plus a load-use stall unit, but full ISA and correctness are not met.

sources.topology: MarkLoveGarry instantiates IF -> ID -> EX -> MEM -> WB. IF uses derived PC_CLK; ID/EX/MEM/WB all run on base clk. PC_CLK pulses once per five base clock edges. This is not a one-clock single-cycle implementation, and has no explicit forwarding, stall or flush logic.

findings.detail: Each stub redeclares the real EX or MEM module. Wildcard compilation of every .v file fails with duplicate module declarations. Keep originals for faithful extraction but exclude these two stubs from any runnable compile set.

MEM declares Alu_result as output reg, never assigns it, and top connects it to the same Alu_result net driven by EX. Intended direction is input; the undriven MEM output introduces an unknown driver and prevents reliable ALU/memory operation.
WB has no reset/initial register values, and ID reads those registers for the first addi (rs=11). Most registers begin X in simulation. MEM reset does not initialize WB registers.
EX implements add/sub/and/or, lw/sw/addi, beq/jump, but no funct 6'b101010 (slt). The supplied ROM contains slt, so loop condition cannot execute.

Jump/branch PC values are hardcoded encoded instruction words, 0x08000019 and 0x8c200000, instead of target addresses. EX.jump is not reset or cleared and remains asserted after a jump. ID's branch commented jump uses opcode 35 (lw) and is unreachable after its earlier lw branch.
The I-type path updates Read_data1 only; sw and beq never read the current rt into Read_data2, so stores/comparisons use a stale operand. Read_Reg1/Read_Reg2 inputs are not used.

ROM differs substantially from slide program: PC8 lw writes r0, PC16 addi writes unavailable r31, PC20 slt writes r1 rather than t2/r2, PC104 OR word has opcode37 instead of R-type opcode0, PC112 AND writes r7 instead of t5/r5, PC116 SW stores r0. These defects are independent of custom register numbering.
Memory recognizes indices 0..10 directly rather than byte addresses 0,4,...40. ROM starts t1 at base+40 then decrements by4, so most intended accesses have no matching memory case.
Top labels s5=r6 ... s0=r11, reversing slide4's explicit s0=r6 ... s5=r11. Consistent custom renaming can be documented, but this does not explain malformed encodings listed above.

Both testbenches only create clock/reset and have no assertions, expected-result checks, or finish condition. finaltb exposes no result wires. A simulator run alone is not evidence that the required instructions work.

level_assessment.B: Five named stages exist, but derived fetch clock and critical defects prevent correctness certification

sources.verdict: Does not elaborate as supplied because top uses two nonexistent named ports. Contains all required opcode cases, but fixed branch/jump targets and value-based forwarding make functional/hazard compliance fail independently of compile blockers.

sources.topology: ha instantiates IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB on the same base clk; instruction and selected datapath values are registered between stages. PC_CLK is produced but IF ignores it and uses clk. No general hazard detector/stall/flush signals. EX has an attempted special cached result substitution for values equal to 2.

findings.detail: Main connects EX using .Alu_result(Alu_result), but EX exposes result. Main connects MEM using .result(result), but MEM exposes Alu_result. Both named ports do not exist; result wire is disconnected from EX and Alu_result is implicitly undeclared until use. The two mismatches prevent elaboration.

Forwarding compares 32-bit operand DATA with 5'b00010 instead of comparing source register addresses with pending destination addresses. Any legitimate value 2 triggers substitution, and dependencies on other values/registers are missed. RESULT is cached only on ins_reg changes when its rd field equals2, without reset or result sensitivity. This cannot satisfy general hazard detection.

IF always jumps to104 and branches to16, ignoring instruction target, offset and current instruction PC; ID's jump extension checks unreachable opcode35 rather than2. No flush/stall accompanies a taken control transfer. This does not implement generic beq/jump semantics.

ROM contains only sub, and, or, add, sw at addresses4..20, then holds the last instruction indefinitely. Actual sequence is sub r2,r1,r3; and r9,r2,r5; or r8,r4,r2; add r7,r2,r2; sw r6,0(r2). It resembles but does not exactly reproduce slide8 Program2 (destinations12/13/14, or source6, store source15 and offset100). It does not exercise lw/addi/slt/beq/jump or the slide's loop example. Presence of all decoder cases alone is not full instruction validation.

Registers use an additional custom map r0 exported as t0 but encoded12, zero encoded31, and s5=r6 ... s0=r11. This differs from slide4. Evaluate as a documented custom subset rather than silently assuming standard ABI numbering.
Testbench drives reset and clock only, with no assertions, expected-result checks or finish. Existing Vivado cache/log files are historical artifacts, not fresh validation of the supplied RTL.

comparisons.normalization_limit: Removing comments and whitespace is a text-similarity check, not formal equivalence.
comparisons.pipeline: 18/19 files normalize to source2 versions. INSTROCTIONMEMORY.v program differs.
comparisons.single_cycle: 14/15 files normalize to source2. InstructionMemory.v program differs.
comparisons.hazard: 8 distinct files form a separate, more monolithic implementation; original top CPU(CLK), no reset port.
important_distinctions: Source2 forwarding independently resolves A/B with per-operand EX priority, whereas source3 globally chooses EX or MEM.
Source2 ALUSrc mux follows forwarding, whereas source3 forwarding follows ALUSrc and can corrupt immediates.
Source2 hazard ALU signed slt returns 0/1, whereas source3 hazard unsigned slt returns 0/0xffffffff.
Source2 hazard addi has unwanted MemWrite=1; source3 hazard fixes MemWrite=0 but selects wrong memory writeback.
Source2 hazard uses array data memory and protected zero register; source3 hazard uses six associative slots and writable zero.

findings.title: addi writes data memory
findings.detail: MEMWRITE is asserted for addi, so an ALU instruction also stores its old rt value to the calculated address.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 addi vs sw semantics

findings.title: Data memory uses byte address as word array index
findings.detail: Both arrays are 64 words but indexed directly by the effective byte address. This implements sparse address slots, restricts legal memory byte addresses to 0..63, and leaves array word63 unreset because reset loop uses i<63. Programs constrained to these addresses can still appear to work.
findings.requirement: Slide 5 MIPS lw/sw addressing; standard MIPS audit assumptions

findings.title: jump absent from pipeline
findings.detail: Controller has no jump output or opcode 000010 case, and top PC mux selects only PC+4 or branch target. Shift-left-26 module is unused.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 j required at every claimed complete ISA level

findings.title: addi writes data memory in pipeline
findings.detail: Controller MEMWRITE remains 1 in addi case, causing unintended stores at MEM stage.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 addi vs sw semantics

findings.title: Pipeline has no data-hazard support or taken-branch flush
findings.detail: IF/ID and ID/EX update every cycle, no forwarding or stall inputs exist, and MEM-stage branch only changes PC without squashing younger instructions. Data dependencies fail without scheduled nops; wrong-path instructions may commit after a taken beq. A basic pipeline can count as structural level B evidence, but cannot claim C or fully correct arbitrary programs.
findings.requirement: Slides 6 pipeline, 7–8 hazards; Slide 2 beq architectural effects

findings.title: jump absent and unsupported opcodes retain old control
findings.detail: Reg controller handles R/lw/sw/addi/beq only, with no j or final default. PC selects branch or PC+4 only. Inserting jump can retain previous instruction controls and perform an unintended write/store.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 j

findings.title: addi selects load-data writeback
findings.detail: addi sets MemtoReg_store=0, which CPU writeback interprets as read_data1 instead of addr1 (ALU result). R-type correctly sets 1, highlighting the mismatch. addi RegWrite=1 therefore writes stale memory-read data.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 addi

findings.title: slt compares unsigned and writes all ones
findings.detail: ALU X/Y are unsigned 32-bit regs; slt returns 0xffffffff when X<Y rather than 1. Negative comparisons also differ from signed slt.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 slt; standard MIPS signed comparison

findings.title: Forwarding selection gives EX/MEM global priority
findings.detail: CPU uses a single EX/MEM if followed by MEM/WB else-if. If EX/MEM matches either operand, MEM/WB forwarding for the other operand is suppressed. Example two older instructions write r1 and r2, then add r3,r1,r2: both different stage values are needed at once.
findings.requirement: Slide 7 forwarding unit

findings.title: Forwarding can replace immediate with rt value
findings.detail: ALU chooses immediate vs register at Y1 first, then forwarding chooses Y2/Y3 after it. CPU forwards based on ID_EX_Rt without ALUSrc gating, even when rt is destination (addi/lw) or store data (sw). Thus matching previous rt overwrites effective-address immediate.
findings.requirement: Slides 2,7 ALUSrc and forwarding semantics

findings.title: Store data bypasses forwarding
findings.detail: EX/MEM captures unforwarded Read_Data2. Forwarded ALU Y does not feed store data and in fact competes with address offset. A producer immediately before sw of its result stores a stale register value.
findings.requirement: Slide 7 forwarding, Slide 2 sw

findings.title: Data memory does not react to address or write-data changes
findings.detail: Dmemory transaction block is sensitive only to memwrite/memread. Consecutive lw or consecutive sw leave controls unchanged and do not retrigger memory handling for their new address/data. This is a direct simulation functional defect and synthesis/simulation mismatch.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 lw/sw

findings.title: Zero register is writable
findings.detail: Register-file write case explicitly assigns Zero <= Writedata for WriteReg=0, violating architectural zero. Forwarding simultaneously ignores register0 destinations, making dependencies inconsistent.
findings.requirement: Standard MIPS audit assumption; not stated verbatim in deck

findings.title: Taken branches do not flush younger instructions
findings.detail: PC branch selection redirects future fetch only; no branch input resets or bubbles IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM. Younger instructions already in flight can commit, up to several wrong-path instructions.
findings.requirement: Slide 2 beq architectural execution

findings.title: Register read port2 maps r30 to sp instead of fp
findings.detail: Second read case 11110 returns sp, while first read case returns fp.
findings.requirement: Standard 32-register MIPS read semantics

findings.title: Original testbenches do not assert correctness
findings.detail: All three TBs drive clocks/reset and end simulation but contain no automated assertions or expected-state comparisons. Running successfully cannot establish compliance. Hazard TB active program only exercises sw,lw,add and one load-use dependency.
findings.requirement: Slide 9 simulation results and top-module TB

findings.title: Unused MUX module has undriven output
findings.detail: MUX.v only declares ports, no output assignment, and is not instantiated by CPU. Preserve as original source but do not count as implemented logic.
findings.requirement: Source quality; unused in active top
